utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I hear and understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, properly attired this afternoon, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good afternoon to you. Yes, preliminaries. I have got a few as well to address to Mr. Ackerman. But please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it goes back to the discussions we had yesterday. Your Honour, because -- well, first of all, we stuck to Witness 7.45 for this Monday because he's here and I would hope that given that he was cross-examined for something like four days in the Stakic case, on matters which effectively are the same as those he's going to testify today, that he can be concluded by the end of the Wednesday sitting. However, because of the moving of the plenary to the 2nd and 3rd of December, we've had to take out Witness 7.46, who is clearly, because as going to be called, in full, a witness of some length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He would have taken four days, that one?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well we estimated the best part of three days because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to offer you - sorry to interrupt you like this - but I was going to offer you to sit on Tuesday, the 3rd as well but I don't think -- unless you have...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour we've got the holiday on the 4th .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've got a holiday on the 4th. No, the 5th, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 5th, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are sitting on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we are committed as I said yesterday to calling Lord Ashdown, because trying to find a window on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Your Honour we've then -- we hope, can I say straight away this is a provisional list because none of these people have YET been contacted to ask if they could come on different days from which originally anticipated. Witness 7.54, we definitely say to be confirmed is because we are having problems with his VISA. Your Honour, I think I ought to stress that the major problem about sudden changes is that the witnesses quite often only get a visa for a limited stay and it takes some time then to reorganise the visa to get them another one for a different date. In addition to that, they make arrangements with their work and it sometimes becomes difficult then to rearrange it. But, Your Honour, that's a provisional list with Your Honours will recall that because the plenary is gone you stated we would be sitting, moved rather the 12th -- the 11th, 12th and 13th. Mr. Ackerman has already made arrangements I understand so we've given this list so that he can clear whether or not these witnesses can be dealt with by his co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yesterday, he confirmed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Everything. Yesterday, you stated that it would be all right for us to sit on the 11th 12th and 13th. He definitely did. First he reserved his position but then later on he came forward and said we could sit the 11th, 12th and 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I said I would consent to sitting on the 11th, 12th and 13th if we started on January 11th, in return.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's one thing I object to, I'm afraid. Your Honour, we had a huge break over the Christmas period. It seems to me, I'm -- I understand, of course and I wouldn't seek for one moment to suggest that the Orthodox -- those of the Orthodox faith shouldn't be allowed to celebrate Christmas on the Monday and Tuesday or whatever it is but there is no good reason that I can see why Mr. Ackerman, for example, couldn't be here on immediately, on the Wednesday to start whether we do intend to call Witness 7.46. In which case we will finish the Prijedor municipality within effectively the first week of sitting. With one caveat to that, Your Honour. You will recall that you gave permission to Mr. Ackerman to deal with the application under Rule 92 in stages but I think the stages ought to come to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's something I was coming to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we need to know whether any of these witnesses will be required immediately after the new year. We've had that request from VWS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go in private session for one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you say something, what I would like you to address also in the course of your intervention is your -- an update on the Rule 92 bis matter and update on the Rule 94 matter, provided that you have been furnished with copies of the transcripts, which I am told you have been, and then finally, there is an application, motion by the Prosecution, 12th motion, on certain protective measures. If I am -- if my calculations are right, I may be wrong, I stand to be corrected, the deadline for your response was yesterday. I don't know if you have filed a response but we haven't had any. We haven't received any. So those are the three things I would like you to address as well, apart from what you had in mind of saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, with regard to those three things, Your Honour, let me -- please give me until Monday and I think I can resolve them all for you by then. They haven't gotten my attention simply because other things have had priority, primarily preparing a number of cross-examinations to be able to proceed this week. And that's mostly what I've done the last seven days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will appreciate especially with regard to 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I fully appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's important for the Prosecution to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As Your Honour knows there is only so many hours in the day there is only so much time I can work. I work hard and I do as much as I can and if I haven't gotten something done it's only because I haven't had time to do it. I don't do other things that detract from my work in this case. As far as the -- I would just like Your Honour to tell all those people out there in the international community who are worried about the progress of our case, that just because we are not sitting in court doesn't mean we are not working. The judges are working, all the lawyers are working. We are all moving this case forward outside the Court just as rapidly as we are moving it forward inside the court and it's not practical for us to sit much more than we can because lawyers simply can't be prepared for much more than the hours we are sitting. And so I think this case is moving forward properly, appropriately, and I think we are all working real hard to make sure that happens and so I don't think we should be subject to any criticism whatsoever, neither this Chamber nor any of the lawyers in it, for the way this case is moving. I think it's being done properly and efficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Incidentally, Mr. Ackerman, and Ms. Korner, I have received just a few minutes before I came up for this sitting, a copy of a letter which I have just read actually, just before walking into the room, from Ms. Martinez with regard to the discussions we had earlier on in the month about resources, additional resources that you had asked to be put in place to assist you to prepare better your Defence. Have you been served with -- have you received this letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That letter is pretty old, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is 8th of November but it only arrived today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've seen the letter and I've had two meetings with Ms. Martinez since then, the latest one being this morning and we are still involved in discussions regarding these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this matter is not concluded as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That letter does not conclude it. Many of the suggestions in there are moot at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I then take -- I'm sorry just to go back to the timetabling. I don't think we had a decision finally because at the moment we need to instruct or get instructions to the person organising the witnesses. We will not be sitting the whole of that week, the first week in January, the 6th to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's my understanding. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next witness is 7.226.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is Mr. Atlija who requires no protective measures, 7.79. Mr. Ackerman originally asked for certain excisions from the transcript which is what you were given. He's since, in the light of the information I've now given him, withdrawn his objection. You should have been handed replacement pages for the ones which were originally redacted and the only basis -- and I have said that I will ask certain follow-up questions to provide further information about some of the things he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you're not happy, we could do away with the sittings of the 13th -- 11th, 12th, 13th of December, schedule to sit starting from Wednesday. That would be 7th of January. Or 8th of January. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, my application was to sit all those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no way we are going to sit all those days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand it's Your Honour's particular circumstances that would make that first week in January as opposed to Mr. Ackerman's objection, that first week in January, difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, Your Honour, I just wanted to confirm that so that we could get the witnesses reorganised again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Usher, could you bring in the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Atlija.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are about to give evidence, testimony, in this case, and before you do so, the usher will be handing you the text of a solemn declaration that you will be telling us the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. So, please, now I invite to you read that solemn declaration out loud and that will be your undertaking to this Trial Chamber that you will be testifying the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is not the first time that you have come to this Tribunal to give evidence. I still welcome you. And I will be very concise and explain to you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- What's going to happen. You are first going to be asked a set of questions by the Prosecution and in this case represented by senior counsel Joanna Korner. She will then be followed by Mr. Ackerman for Radoslav Brdjanin, who is the accused here, in what we refer to as a cross-examination. I am also to inform you that we have available the transcript of your testimony in the Stakic case and what you stated -- what you testified in that case will also form part of the records of this case. However, you will be asked questions which may be in addition to what you testified in that case, but also with reference to what you testified. Ms. Korner, he is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, can we just establish your identity and background for the purposes of the record? I think your full name is Ivo Atlija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were born on the 19th of May, 1963, in Brisevo, which is in the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You are, by nationality and ethnic origin, a Croat?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And a Roman Catholic by religion?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, as you're aware I'm going to just summarise the evidence that you gave when you testified in the case against Dr. Milomir Stakic, which I think you yourself have had a chance to review by listening to the tapes of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First I'd like to you have a look, please, at a map so that we can just show the judges where Brisevo is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we will use this one because it's -- I don't think it's one of Mr. Inayat's maps but I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we have -- at least what it seems that we have --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is S184A in Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is a clear enough map.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, I think we've got a coloured version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case we will use that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly and I don't think he needs to point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could Your Honour just hold up that particular map which one that was? We are having some difficulty ourselves in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When we have is a black and white -- it's a very simple map, rudimentary with a lot of arrows.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, that's not it. Would Your Honour forgive me for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, I think what we will do is -- this map has already been exhibited as -- all right. We will look for the exhibit number. Can we just put it on the ELMO so everybody can see what we are looking at? All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, just so we look at it, we can see Prijedor, the town, and then can we see Ljubija to the southwest?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: This is Ljubija here, Donja Ljubija and Gornja Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we find Brisevo? We may need to move the map up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That's where I was born and where I grew up. This area here is called Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Move it up.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: [In English] It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did Brisevo come within the commune of Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was part of the Ljubija local community.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this, Your Honours, appears at page 5546 - you can take the map away, thank you very much, usher - on the transcript at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it was a village of approximately 120 houses?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And apart from some women of Serb ethnicity who were married to Croats, all the other inhabitants were Bosnian Croat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, about 400 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And as we are going to see and hear, I think it contained a Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That is also true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, let's just go through, then, please, and I'm going to ask you to look at photographs and videos during the course of this summary, you told us -- you told the Court in Stakic about your background and your military service and that you worked after your military service had finished at a repair shop for the Ljubija mines?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. The workshop was usually referred to as the central workshop.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, I'm just summarising, you described the interethnic relationship before and after 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm moving to page 5549.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then the propaganda that was put out, which began to change the nature of the relationship?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You described the increase in the carrying of weapons that took place shortly in the months before the takeover, and then I think you described the takeover in Prijedor on the 30th of April, after which you were sent home from your work and returned to your village in Brisevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, may I interrupt to say that the map I put on the ELMO was in fact P1127 so that we know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You described --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is at page 5555 onwards --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- your witnessing of the attacks on Hambarine and Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the announcements that you heard on Prijedor Radio being made on behalf of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's at page 5559, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You described on the 27th of May the shelling of Brisevo, which came from Serb villages, and the ultimatum that was given to you, your village, to surrender all your weapons, including a gun they thought you had called a Bofors gun, although you had no such weapon. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I do, and you put it quite accurately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you described how Brisevo was blockaded and you were unable to leave, to obtain either food or medical supplies. And you described some incidents where people were arrested before the attack on Brisevo and taken to camps. Now I just want to ask you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm now going to page 5569. This was originally one of the pages where excisions took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us last time, in the Stakic case, about an attack on, first of all, on sorry, on a man named Milan Ivandic, who was beaten and cut with a screwdriver. Do you remember telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You didn't witness this yourself, but who told you about this incident?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I first learned about it from Milan Buzuk, but the news spread very quickly by word of mouth, as is usually the case in villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how long after this incident did Milan Buzuk tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: A day later, a day after it happened, I already knew what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just so the Defence know, what happened to Mr. Buzuk?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Mr. Buzuk was tortured and killed in the course of the attack on Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then after that, you described at some length the actual attack on Brisevo which began at about half past 3.00 a.m. on the 24th of July; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this was an attack that took place without any warning whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it was, as you discovered, an attack by two separate units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is at page 5585.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The 6th Krajina Brigade and the 5th Kozara Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think you received confirmation of this at a meeting that you later had with Mr. Vojo Kupresanin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you witnessed a number of killings personally which you described, and I think you also drew a number of sketch plans to illustrate the evidence you were giving. The first one --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was referred to at page 5580. And I think we better give you that so you can just -- it was annex D, that's it, yes. Could that be given to the witness, put up on the ELMO? Your Honours, just before that does, I wasn't quite sure what the outcome of the discussion was other than each document was to be given a new exhibit number for this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think what we are going to do - I had a very short discussion with Madam Chuqing before we started the sitting - is that in order to lessen the possibility of confusion as much as we could, we are creating a new number that would be the exhibit number in this case but then we will be preserving, keeping, the Stakic reference number, separating the two with a dot. So it would be, for example, 1516.the number in Stakic, is that how you proposed it, Madam Chuqing?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would that be accepted by the OTP. I think that would save us a lot of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it will be easier for us later on because what is going to happen, Ms. Korner is this: We will -- I would imagine -- out of these many witnesses that we have, coming from Stakic, with transcripts, we are going to be reading those or quoting from those for the purposes of the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there will be references to the documents as numbered in Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we give them a completely different number in Brdjanin, that could create a confusion even as far as tallying is concerned. So what has been suggested to me, I agreed to, or I agreed with, because I think it will lessen the possibilities, reduce the possibilities of confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what -- yes, I'm perfectly content with that. For example, this one, which was S183, if we could call that P1522/S183?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Your Honours, I hope we don't need because we handed out the documents if Your Honour could just write them over the top or the registry can write.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can move along without any problems like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that case -- has the witness now got it? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you just so the Court can see, just very briefly summarise what you showed on this drawing?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: On this drawing in front of us, I described and marked the place where Pero Dimac was killed and in the text I described the incident and I put a small cross with initials PD, that is the place where he was killed and another small cross with IA, that is my name, and VT, VT, Viktor Tozan these are the two places, these marked these indicate two places where we were hiding and from which we saw Pero Dimac being killed and I also drew some houses just to provide for a better orientation to show you what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So where we can see is where you've marked other people's houses?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. That's just for the sake of orientation so that you know where the site of the murder was in relation to the church and other buildings in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. So can we now look at the second map that you drew in respect of military units? That was page 55 -- annex E. Yes, thank you. Would you look at that, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will then become Exhibit P1523/S184. Your Honour, this was referred to at page 5585 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just again show -- we can see you've marked various troop movements. If you just indicate what you were showing there?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: On this drawing, I tried, and I wasn't alone, I didn't do it all by myself, we tried to reconstruct the attack on Brisevo and the direction from which the units of the 5th Kozara unit came and from which direction the units of the 6th Krajina Brigade came. I can show you from south, from the Sava bridge, the units of the 6th Kozara Brigade were moving, mostly through the villages of Ostra Luka and Rasavci to this side here and from the direction of Ljubija and Prijedor, that is from the north, the units that belonged to the 5th Kozara Brigade were advancing and somewhere in the centre of Brisevo, they came together and thus closed the circle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. That's very helpful, Mr. Atlija. You can put that one away. Now, I think you went back to Brisevo after the attack had concluded, and after the infantry had been in and you described the deaths, the looting. I want to look now -- you described the level of destruction, and I think you said that some 68 houses had been burnt and the church had been virtually destroyed, and I want to you have a look, please, now, at some photographs that you were shown as well, just to identify them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, those were 185, yeah, in the Stakic case. Thank you. Just put them up on the ELMO, one by one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First photograph?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, for reference that's page 5591 of the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is -- shows what?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It shows the Catholic church in Brisevo, built in 1990. At the time, when it was photographed, I believe it had not yet been officially opened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The next photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: On this photograph, we see the remains of a house owned by Antika Mlinar, Ante or Antika. We just called him Antika but whether his true name is Ante or Antika, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then can we look, please, at the next photograph?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: This photograph shows what remains of the houses owned by Nedo Mlinar and Andjelko Mlinar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: This photograph also shows what remains of Antika Mlinar's house from a different angle. The photograph was taken from a different place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the photograph after that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: This could be what remains of the Matic's family house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we look at the next photograph, with the number 4764, I think that shows a closeup taken from above?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. This photograph was taken from above, from a higher altitude, from the road, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then can we look at the next, please? 4765?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I think that here you see what remains of the house which I think belonged to Stipe Dimac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally, 4766?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: This I think is the same building but the photograph was taken from a different angle, from a different place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. That will then be P1524/S-- what? I think it's 24. We've had two diagrams and if they can be -- it will be a collection point 1, whatever the photographs are. I think there are six altogether. Next could I ask you, please, to have a look at the video that you saw before? We've shortened it because it shows a lot of Ljubija. I just want you to look, please, at the church. This was filmed, I think, by a German television crew so if we could just play that video, from the point where it was set up? Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we stop, please, stop the video? Sorry, freeze it. I'm sorry, I should have said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, I think as last time if you just say to stop the video and they will freeze the frame. So if we could go back to the frame?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes exactly let's rewind a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then when you want us to freeze the screen, please tell us what's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Freeze. This is where you can see very well what remains of the church. This is the same the one that we saw in the photographs. This is taken from the front door towards the interior of the church.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we carry on playing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, here we should see the roof of the church which is gone. I mean it burnt down and caved in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the interior of that church. I don't think there is any need to freeze it. I mean if it is moving so slowly then there is no need to stop every time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, just carry on playing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can see where the so-called altar was. That is, you see what remains of the cross on the wall. This is the remains -- what remains of the belfry, again taken from the inside. This is the front door, taken from inside, and to the left, the staircase leading to the choir. That is where the choir usually is during the mass, during service.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The belfry once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we see the bell, or rather the pieces of the -- of the bell, which fell down and broke. And around it we see the brick, tiles of those that fell inside when the roof fell down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you very much. I think that will do. Your Honour, that will be P1525/S186.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you then described to the Court -- you told the Court that some 68 people had been killed, and you then described to the Court the various burials that you took part in around the area, and you drew -- you used for those purposes, again, another diagram, and I wonder if you could now look at that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, there is a slight hitch. Just a moment. I think I've got another copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, we used the same map. That's right. It's whatever it is, Exhibit -- annex E, which was Exhibit P1523 -- 1523/184. That's it. Could we have that back? Yeah. That's right. And I now recall because he did draw another map but it was very unclear so we used this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think first of all, you described how you buried your father, who was killed?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you dealt with the various bodies and graves that you dug. First of all, I think at Stara Rijeka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which you can see on the left of that plan. Now, I need to ask you about that, because that was related to some people who passed through your village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was at page 5601. It was again one of the original excisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You didn't see a group of Muslims passing through your village, I think, but were you told about it. Can you remember now who told you about it?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I didn't see them personally and I cannot remember who it was exactly who told me at that time that some ten or 12 Muslims had passed through our village and moved towards Stari Majdan across through Stara Rijeka, I'm sorry, I just can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all right. I just thought I'd check. Then I think you described to the court, this is page 5602 -- you found some remains, people you recognised, and that was at a hamlet called Dimaci; is that correct? And if you just point to that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct, and I'll point at it. It's a very small here but you can still here that it says Dimaci.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And one of the people you described was a gentleman named Stipo Dimac who was between, you thought, 76 to 78 years old. Then I think you described bodies at the hamlet of Mlinari and again if you can just point that out?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, there you described how you heard from eyewitnesses that the people who had been killed had been made to dig their own graves and had then been killed with the tools. That's at page 5604. Can you tell us who told you about that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It is true that I said that, and it was described. One of the survivors who witnessed that event, her name is Zdenka Lovric. She's now married and changed her last name. Now, she's Dimac and her mother Mara Lovric was also present and some ten or 12 women and children more but their names, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think you yourself witnessed the injuries. Obviously you can't tell us because you're not a medical man, which of the injuries caused death. Then I think that you described bodies in Buzuci, in front of Marko Buzuk's house and he was the man you mentioned earlier, I think?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's right. That is the father of the mentioned Milan Buzuk who first told me about the unfortunate event with Milan Ivandic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then I think you described at page 5607 the hamlet of Mustanica and there I think you buried Pero Dimac and your father; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. That's true. That's about here. It's a stream called Mustanica. It flows towards Stara Rijeka and that is how that part of the village got its name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think you also described finding the body of a man named Ante Matanovic who had been killed, you thought, with a firearm. You identified a bullet wound. Were you familiar with bullet wounds as a result of your military service?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I know what bullet wounds look like. The entry wound is about the width of a finger and there is a little bit of blood. The exit wound is the size of a fist and it's of an irregular shape. This is generally what bullet wounds look like and this is what I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then you described, I think, the -- some graves at a hamlet called Ivandici which I don't think was on the map. Could you point it out? I think you pointed it out last time.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It's not marked on the map but I will indicate it. It is somewhere in this area. If you go from the direction of Brisevo towards the village called Zecovi it's on the right side. Straight ahead is Kurevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you described a grave near Ivo Zunic's house in the hamlet of Cengije.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Cengije.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Cengije, thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Cengije.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you can indicate that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I can indicate that. It's not marked. It is before the house that we mentioned a little while ago. There is only one house indicated here but the hamlet of Cengije would be approximately here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you described to the Court on the last occasion, this is page 5610, that there had been women in the graves, in particular somebody called Kaja Komljen, and you described that eyewitnesses said that other people, Luka Komljen and his son had been tortured. Can you just tell us who told you that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Drago Zunic was the eyewitness as well as his wife. I'm not sure what her name is. I think her name is Jelena.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then you described some graves on the Raljas hill. If you can just indicate that on the map?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It is marked on the map. The peak of the hill, Raljas. We can see it here. The graves are a little lower. The marked road is on the map. There are some houses there. There is a stream a little bit above that. So one group of graves was on one side of the stream and another group of graves was on the other side of the stream.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think you find there -- you found a 14 year old, Luka Mlinar, buried in one. Was he somebody that you knew as a neighbour?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I knew him from the day he was born, from the day he was born. He's younger than I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then was there also another boy called Mirsad Svraka. Can you just tell us how you were able to identify who that was?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That boy was not someone we knew but we found his identity card in his clothes so all his particulars were contained in that card, the first and last name, the date of birth and et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then I think you described some graves in Redak. Can you just indicate on the map where the Redak grave is?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I can point it out. The name is Redak. This area here is called Redak. These are the remains of a mine. There are still some remains of ore that was mined there. The road forks to Gornji Ravska on one side and Brisevo on the other and then it continues in the direction of Stara Rijeka, Stari Majdan, Sanski Most and so on. The grave itself was at the fork in the road. There were some large truck tires nearby. It wasn't really a grave. It was just a pile of bodies thrown one on top of another.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that then deals with that. Can you look, please, now, briefly at a video you saw last time as well, which is part of the video that Mr. Inayat shot? I just wanted --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was referred to at page 5632. And again if you want to point something out, perhaps just say "stop." If we could play that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. In this part of the footage, you can see the elementary school in Ljubija, a little bit to the right, in the frame, you can see the premises, the changing rooms of the football club. I can't remember whether that was the name of it but I think it was the soccer club. To the left is the playing field, the soccer field, and next to the field and the school, the road continues and leads to the settlement or the town of Ljubija itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We can carry on playing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. In this frame, I think you can see the factory which I think was called Tomeks, the Tomeks factory which is a factory for the construction of -- or the production of metal and explosives. I think it was a relatively new factory and I think that that was what it produced.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. At this point, I think you can see in the background of the frame the low hills of the Kozara. In front of it is Prijedor. Then you can see some mist in the front or clouds. That is approximately where the river Sana flowed, and these along the river were villages which were in inhabited 100 per cent by Serbs, the villages of Rasavci all the way to Ostra Luka and so on so from that direction towards the front, towards Brisevo, is where the members mostly of the 6th Krajina Brigade came and all the way to the left from Prijedor towards Ljubija and Raljas is where the members of the 5th Ljubija Brigade came from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. Here in this picture, you can see very well the remains of the burnt and demolished houses. This is the house that was owned by Nedo Mlinar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. Here you can see the remains of the house that was owned by Andjelko Mlinar, and on the left are the remains of the house owned by Vlado Mlinar, Nedo Mlinar's son. In the background you can see hills. That is where the border is between Brisevo and Rasavci to the left and -- to the right and Ostra Luka to the left and that is the direction from where the infantry came.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. Here on the -- in the upper right-hand corner you can see the remains of the school in Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. Also to the right, on the right side of the screen, you can see the remains of a church. You can see the bell tower and then you can also see the road which leads to the Marijani hamlet. If you continued straight ahead, you would arrive at Sanski Most. On the right side is the village of Raljas, and then further is Ljubija and from that side, from that direction, is where the members of the 5th Kozara Brigade came from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. On the right side, across from the church, you can see, not so clearly, but you can see the remains of the house of Jozo Jakara. He was killed right next to the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour that will be P1526/S58.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now just to then really conclude, Mr. Atlija, the summary, you described to the Court that armed men came to Brisevo, even after the attack, and you described then how you heard about the women who were raped in Brisevo immediately after the attack. And you gave the ages. Your Honours, this is at page 5640. Again, it was one that was originally redacted. How did you hear about the rapes?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It was very difficult to get information from the women themselves about what happened, but the members of their families and from what we were able to see of their injuries, it could be concluded which women were raped. Some of them tried to commit suicide. However, because of their conservative Catholic upbringing and because of some prejudices, and I cannot speak for others, but I believe that the majority of them will never state publicly anywhere that they had been raped.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you talk about their injuries, are you talking about external and internal injuries?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I am talking about both external and internal injuries. The physical injuries could be cured or healed, treated in some way, but their traumas, I don't know what the expert terminology would be for that, but the psychological consequences of what they had gone through are something that we could not help them with. There were no psychiatrists or any experts who at that point in time could help those women with their experiences. So it was very difficult to do anything for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you able to obtain the necessary sort of medical supplies to treat those injuries?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We didn't receive any kind of medical supplies from anybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then I think you described the two visits to the area by Vojo Kupresanin and Bishop Komarica amongst others. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you described at page 5643 the speech that Mr. Kupresanin made to the assembled people there. And I think you personally spoke to him.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's right. I did talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as you said earlier, he was the one who confirmed the units of the military that were involved in the attack.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's right. He confirmed that they were, in fact, the 6th Kozara and the 5th Krajina Brigade and as regards to all the crimes, he did say that this was a small group which was not under anybody's control. When I asked him how was it possible that two brigades would escape anybody's control, he didn't respond to my question. He didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think that he also said that he would do everything in respect of General Talic so that the situation would end?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct. He said that he would personally intervene with General Talic, that things like this have to stop, that we will live with one another again and all of these things will stop as soon as they occupied the Tuzla industrial centre, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think he made the suggestion that you should go and speak to Dr. Stakic who was president of the Municipal Assembly, as you understood it, or the Crisis Staff, and I think you and others went as a delegation to him without much success?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's right. He directed us to Mr. Stakic and he also recommended that we should telephone to Ljubija, to the headquarters of the Serb command that was situated in Ljubija. However, we didn't manage to achieve anything through this. There were no results.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Eventually, did you leave the area for Zagreb on the 17th of November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct. On the 17th of November, 1992, I crossed over into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before leaving, I think you had to pay, Your Honours this is page 5655 -- you had to pay electricity, phone and other utility bills and you were actually paying for things you didn't have, such as a phone, and did you also have to sign a document saying that you were leaving of your own free will and some kind of a certificate leaving your property to the disposal of -- you weren't quite clear whether it was the Republika Srpska or the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. I'm not sure what that entity or region at that time was officially called but we did have to sign, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Atlija, have you ever been back to Brisevo since these events of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I went to Brisevo during the exhumation of those killed at Brisevo, and their burial, and later, I visited again the graves of those killed in Brisevo. However, no one has returned to live in Brisevo. People occasionally go to visit the graves there but then they go back to wherever they are now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can't answer for others, but why haven't you personally gone back to try and restart your life again there?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: One of the reasons, one of very important reasons why people are not going back there and will not go back there and why I personally will not go back there as long as the entity called Republika Srpska exists is as follows: As long as people who are in power there and in Prijedor who organised, planned and took part in all of these crimes, they are again in power, they are again police officers, judges, and they occupy other posts, we do not trust such people and we have a saying that a person, once bitten, twice shy. So that is the reason why we will not go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Atlija.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, we are due to break in any case in five minutes' time. Shall we take the break now and you start straight afterwards? We need to finish today at 6.00 to enable the interpreters in particular to attend a special function so may I suggest to you that we restrict the break to 20 minutes? All right? Or 15 minutes? 15 minutes. Is it okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm just wondering we've got a second witness coming today, are we likely to get to that second witness today? If we are stopping at 6.00? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I imagine so. So 15 minutes, all right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before Mr. Ackerman cross-examines, two matters. First, I'm told I misunderstood the way that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's all right. She has told me you may proceed, Ms. Chuqing has told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For today, we will have to stick to this but we will go back to the old system for the next witness but, Your Honour, I didn't make the transcript an exhibit which is P1527.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to draw your attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In addition to that, Your Honour, what unfortunately we left behind which I only realised when I was checking was Mr. Atlija looked at three other photographs which we haven't shown him this time. We are going to get them and we'll just attach them. They are self explanatory in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My bundle, I do have about four other photos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You do, do you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With grave and the fields.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours do have it. For some reason it seems to have escaped us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have about four. If they have escaped you. I can imagine what Mr. Ackerman is going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You have them too. In that case I'm quite happy then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have one, two, three, four -- four other photos that he was not shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wonder for a moment. I hate to ask this, does the registry have those as well? If not, can I just borrow Your Honour's bundle for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. These are the four photos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thanks. Oh, yes. That's right. Having said to Mr. Ackerman -- can I just show them to the witness and he can identify them for Your Honours it makes things easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we can just take these -- we did have them and I just missed them. Perhaps if we can show them now to the witness and just get him to identify them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, I didn't mention anything before because I imagined that you were coming to them later on during your --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just couldn't find them in the bundle I was clutching.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, can you just tell the Court again what we can see there?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: This photograph could be the place at Redak where I mentioned there was a pile of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the next?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: This is the so-called Raljas cemetery where the majority of those killed at Brisevo were buried.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the next? I think there we see -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: This photograph was taken at the same cemetery and you can see gravestones. On one is my father Ilija Atlija, Jozo Jakara and Stipo Dimac. They are all the people whom I mentioned in my earlier statement about -- that they had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think there is one more or is that the lot? Yes. Are you able to identify that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, this is not really clear but one can glean, I think, the remains of the church.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, right at the top. Yes, thank you. Yes, thank you very much, Mr. Atlija?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour can they just be added to the photographs -- yes, the photographs, P1524 with the Stakic numbers and the transcript? I think I've already done 1527.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm wondering while we are dealing with photographs if the witness might be shown that series that he was shown earlier the S185 series starting with number 2 through 8, I believe, it would be 47, 60 through 66, I think are the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I don't need to put these on the ELMO. I'd like you to -- the one that I'm not concerned about, that's the photograph of the church, the balance of those photographs that we saw showing buildings that had been destroyed and damaged, do you -- do you know when those photographs were taken?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It appears by looking at them that they were taken quite a long time after the events. For instance, look for instance at S185-8 it's got a number 4766 probably the last photograph in the batch. It looks like it's been so long that trees have grown up inside that building, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. It is. But you know, when something burns, ash is produced and ash is a substance which boosts the fertility of the soil so that I cannot really say whether this was taken six months later or two years later, ten years later. I can't really tell you because I wasn't the one who took those photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you think you can grow a 12-foot tree in six months? A 3-metre tree, 4-metre tree?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how tall is this tree. I just mentioned as an example. I can't really say six months later a year or two years later. I really cannot answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well if you just look at the photograph, sir, there is leaves coming out the top where the roof would have been. That has to be at least four metres high, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I see that the leaves are at about the roof level but how tall that is, again, I cannot tell you but to me it is relevant, some plants grow faster, some grow slower. I'm not an expert on these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stop this. Point taken, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Move to the next --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, between the 18th and 20th of October of the year 2000, you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. You recall doing that, I take it?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me just tell you now that if at any time during the questions I have about that you would like to consult that statement and look at it, I can arrange for you to have it. So just tell me if you'd like to have it, okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest we have it ready and give it to him straight away rather than waste time later on, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would be fine with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So usher, please. Which statement are you referring to the one of the 18th to 20th October?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So please, usher, could you hand the witness that statement, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The part I want to speak about first is -- it's actually the second page of your statement. It has the number 3 on it, in the English version. Where you told the investigator from the Tribunal, "I have attended several conferences where the topic of discussion was the Bosnian war." You say they were mainly attended by journalists, local politicians and refugees. We never talked of specific incidents but focused primarily on the general situation in Bosnia before the war. In some of those conferences, I too addressed the participants." Okay?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where were these conferences held?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They were all held in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And where in Germany?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: In Germany, around Frankfurt, that is all I can tell you. They were so-called jugendhaus, which is youth hostels, in some small places in villages in localities where young people would gather in the presence of local politicians and journalists and they talked about politics and war. They mostly looked like some workshops, like roundtables rather than conferences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, if you will listen to my questions, and just answer the question I ask you, we will be finished here much quicker. My question was where in Germany were the conferences held and let's try to do that, and if you want to elaborate on an answer I'm certainly going to let you do that but you should try to answer my question as quickly and easily as you can, okay?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: One of the places where such a conference was held is called Ingelheim near Mainz. I don't know the names of all those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Who sponsored these conferences?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I'm afraid I might go wrong but I think that at least one of those conferences was organised -- it was called Hessische Landespolitische Zentralle or something like that. But I suppose some others participated too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you said in your statement that you actually spoke at some of these conferences. How many of the conferences were you -- did you actually speak at?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Three, maybe four. I'm afraid to give you a wrong figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was your speech about? What did you talk about at each of these conferences?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Those conferences discussed generally the relations in Europe. For instance, what the relations were on the eve of World War II or after it, the relations in the Balkan peninsula in the former Yugoslavia, the relations before the war broke out, the possibilities for reinstating some more or less normal state of affairs. And then people confronted our opinions. Of course there were different opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm a bit confused about and just see if you can help me, will you? First of all, you told the --

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I shall be happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: First of all you told the Prosecutor's investigators that you attended several conferences where the topic of discussion was the Bosnian war. Now, I assume that would have been the war in 1992 and thereafter, when you say the topic of discussion was the Bosnian war, that would be the war you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Mostly, principally about the war in Bosnia, perhaps I wasn't precise enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, but then the next thing you said was that it was focused primarily on the general situation in Bosnia before the war. Now, which one of those was it? It was a discussion about the events before the war or was it a discussion about the events during the war?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, the most correct answer would be if I told you that the -- that the attention was principally paid to the causes which brought about the war in Bosnia, the causes, different political stances, different political influences. Those were the things that relate -- the chief emphasis on and we discussed very little some combat operations on the ground and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us who Luka Gavranovic is?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I met Luka Gavranovic in 1993. At that time I know that he worked for the Croatian information bureau in Zagreb and he was one of those to whom I gave one of my first statements about the developments in Brisevo. Whether he was the chief of that centre or whether he was just an ordinary official, rank and file official, I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What is the Croatian information centre?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Croatian information centre is an organisation which collected information about the war in Bosnian Croatia, excuse me in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia. Whether it still exists, whether they still do that or is it perhaps some other organisation today, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you never worked for that centre or was -- you were never a part of that centre? Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It is, yes. I never worked for any such organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This -- the map that is Prosecution Exhibit 1523/S184, that's -- I don't know if you -- you probably don't know the map I'm talking about, you probably ought to be able to see it. So would you take a look at it, please? P1523/S184. It's annex E to the documents. You know which map I'm speaking of now, don't you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the case, isn't it, that this Luka Gavranovic assisted you in the drawing and preparation of this map?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it that means that much of the information contained on this map, especially regarding these various units, was information that Mr. Gavranovic claimed to know, that you weren't certain about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's divide the question into two parts, Mr. Ackerman, because in one part you are alleging and asking the witness to confirm or deny that Mr. Gavranovic or whatever his name claimed to know, and secondly, you are also alleging that the witness wasn't certain about these facts, which may not be the case. So I would suggest to you that you either rephrase the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- or you separate it into two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Parts of this map were based on information that Mr. Gavranovic claimed to know about, weren't -- isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say yes or no. Mr. Gavranovic helped me to draw this map but more technical matters, drawing the map, the distances and some of the features. As for the facts from which direction, which unit advanced, whether this is the 6th Krajina or the 5th Kozara, which battalion, those were some things I heard from some officers who were not far from places where I hid or from some eyewitnesses, the survivors in Brisevo. These facts are the facts that I knew, not something that Mr. Gavranovic knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So nothing on here was information given to you by Mr. Gavranovic but all information that you had knowledge of either personally or that you had heard from someone?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. Mr. Gavranovic received information from me rather than the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go back to your statement now on a different matter. On the next page, after the one we referred to, there is a paragraph that begins with, "I was never a member of any political party." And then what you tell the investigator is, "Before the war, the interethnic relations amongst different groups was extremely good."

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were from Brisevo, right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic makeup of Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, 100 per cent Croats, a few Serb women married to Croats. They also lived in Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you told us a little earlier, looking at one of the photographs that showed mist apparently rising up from the river, that all the villages along that river were Serb villages, correct? 100 per cent Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Almost 100 per cent. I also know that there were some mixed marriages but mostly, not mostly, almost 100 per cent -- the population of these villages were almost 100 per cent Serbs that you can see on that photograph but if we move to the left, with the -- to where you can't see on the photograph, Carakovo, Biscani, Hambarine, Rizvanovici, and so on and so forth, and their population was almost 100 per cent Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There were several villages, the Kozarac area, Jakupovici, those areas, Trnopolje down there, that were 100 per cent Muslim, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's right. They were across the Sana on the other bank the Sana, the foot hills of Kozara and this is from this part -- this side of the Sana, towards Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question is this: If interethnic relations amongst the different groups was extremely good, why were they all living apart from each other like that, why were they living separately, ghetto-ed apart from each other?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The villages were almost ethnically pure but the distance between those villages was not big. They attended the same schools, worked for the same companies, played basketball or football together or practised karate and other sports. I did not notice during those years before the war that the ethnic relations were disrupted in any way. We played instruments together, played music together, danced together, played various games together and I'd say that these relations were good. Why the villages were Serb or Muslim or Croat almost 100 per cent, well, to tell you the truth I'd never really given it a thought before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that was the case in 1989 and in 1989, everybody knew that there were villages that were Muslim villages that were Croat and villages that were Serb, didn't they? That wasn't something that came about as a result of the elections or the war or anything else, right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The elections before the unfortunate war in the former Yugoslavia were no elections, because you could vote only for representatives nominated by the then League of Communists of Yugoslavia or somebody against them. There were no democratic elections in which you could properly elect freely and democratically amongst a number of candidates and amongst a number of political options.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I didn't ask you about the elections. I'm going to give up on the question I actually asked you because I think you've already answered it. Page -- the same page of your statement, you were asked to give an example of Serb propaganda and the example you came up with was this: "Once in 1991, the Prijedor Radio announced that a Muslim doctor, Mirza Mujadzic had given injections to pregnant Serb women so that they would give birth to girls and in this way, reduce the Serb male population." That's what you said, right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. And it spread very fast indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It spread, such things, such news spread very fast by word of mouth. That kind of propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you actually hear that announcement?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you -- do you personally know anybody that believed that? Do you know anybody that's dumb enough to believe that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, regrettably, there were some people working with me who did believe those things. Unfortunately. I repeat it once again. And we tried to tell them that if somebody had such an injection he would win the Nobel Prize for medicine because it does not exist in the world. However their heads, their heads were full of such things. They simply could not not believe it, and they adhered to that, they held on to it, as if it was a sacrosanct thing. That is so and it must be so. I mean it is regrettable but it is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Male, females, according to the temperature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not -- if the temperature is constantly hotter than usual, then they produce only females. If the temperature drops, they produce males. So Mr. Mirza Mujadzic may have taken the idea from there. Yes. Let's go -- let's proceed, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that aside, Your Honour. I don't know whether to say I appreciate it but thank you for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Couldn't you just look around and see, sir, women going around with boy babies? Wouldn't that kind of obvious that it was not true?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I could, but it didn't have anything to do with me, with what I could see or what I believed in because I didn't decide on anything. It was more important what other people believed in and what other people advocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So basically it was Serbs that were believing this story?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: When I say Serbs, please do not take it that I mean all Serbs. I do not think that all the Serbs in the world believe something like that. Either in Serbia or in Bosnia or in Prijedor but I'm saying that some Serbs who worked with me and I can't remember all the names, after all it was ten years ago so many things have faded away even in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I think we've talked about that enough. Let's go to -- I'm now going to page 12 of your statement. And I'm in the English version so I'm not sure where it is in B/C/S version but it deals with soldiers you saw, the paragraph I'm talking about: "The soldiers I that saw were wearing very narrow red armbands." The part of that I want to refer you to is the very last sentence of that paragraph. You said, "All the officers spoke in an Ekavian dialect which is spoken in mainland Serbia. However, this does not mean that these officers were from mainland Serbia because I know that the official dialect used in the former JNA was the Ekavian dialect," correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It is correct. I did my military service with the JNA and the official language, yes, was the Serbian dialect, the Ekavian dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You speak in there of seeing four or five officers and you say that you could tell that they were officers by the insignia they were wearing on their epaulettes, the officer insignia on their epaulettes. Do you know in war situations whether officers remove those rank insignia so they will not be identified as officers? Do you know whether that happens or not?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
