utterances.text: Not only that this happens. It was a rule. It was a rule in the Yugoslav People's Army, at least when I served in it. And that is why it struck me that those people had not removed the epaulettes from the shoulders, they still -- they kept them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. On the same page, talking about the attack and the units involved, the very last paragraph on page 12, you simply mention that you saw no policemen involved in the attack, and that's also the case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I didn't see police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to now talk with you for just a moment about the statement that you actually gave to the Croatian information centre. The statement itself indicates -- it's dated January 30, 1993, which I think indicates the date that that statement was given, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And a great deal of what you said in that statement was based upon what you'd been told by other people and not your own personal knowledge, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It's true that there are parts that are based on information I received from other people, but in my statements here I tried to separate what I personally saw and experienced and what I heard from somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. The point I will make, and I think you'll agree with me, is that you later learned that a number of the things that you had said in that statement, based on what other people had told you, were simply not correct, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I don't remember stating that there were things that were not true in my statements. I don't remember that it says anywhere here that something that is in the statement was not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, look, for instance, -- do you have that statement? Is it attached to the one that you were given? It was in my...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher? Did you give the witness his statement to the Croatian information centre?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's annex A with the ERN number 01056384.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to look at page 3 and I have a few questions about that page. It's page 3 in the English version. It's underneath the paragraph that says, "16th grave." The paragraph begins with the language, "As to the Brisevo casualties."

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says, "As to the Brisevo casualties, we found out about the ways in which they were murdered." When you use the word "we," does that include you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Not in all of these 68 cases, regarding all of the 68 persons killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you say, "We found out," you may be referring to other people and not yourself? You're not part of that "we"?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: With the majority of those killed out of those 68 people, I was present when they were buried. So with most of them, I could see the cause of death, but not with all of them. I stress that. And when I say "we" here, I mean us survivors who buried those people but I did not attend every single funeral. That is also stated somewhere in the statement. I said that I was not present at every single funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I totally understand that. Look at the next paragraph, it begins with the name Milan Buzuk. You say about that, "When we found him." Did you find him? Or did someone else find him?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Milan Buzuk, his mother was the first person to see where he was killed. Naturally she fled from that place and later Franjo Mlinar, Viktor Tozan, myself, Branko Atlija and someone else found him. I was present then and I saw everything very clearly and all the facts are known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the paragraph that begins with the name "Ivica Mlinar," just a couple more paragraphs down, in the middle of that paragraph you make this statement: "First they would sever their muscles and tendons so that a victim was in no position to escape or defend himself/herself." You've said subsequent that that part of your statement was not correct, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I think that there is a small misunderstanding here. I didn't say that a part of the statement was not true but maybe that it was unfortunately termed. I didn't mean that they cut off the muscle or remove it from the body, but I'm talking about the wounds indicating that the tendon was severed which would separate the muscle from the bone so that the person is unable to move that limb any more, is unable to defend themselves to offer resistance or to flee and I think somewhere later, I explained this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go, please, to about two pages later, the paragraph begins with, "Beside the above-mentioned 6th Krajina Brigade," it's a long paragraph.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of that paragraph, you say this: "The 6th Krajina Brigade numbered 3500 armed men at the time." Now, the fact is that you have no idea what the number of armed men in the 6th Krajina Brigade at the time was. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That was my assumption. I did not know then, nor do I know now, exactly how many people there were in the 6th Krajina Brigade. This is based on the knowledge I gained in the JNA; what is part of a platoon, a company, a unit, a brigade, a corps. That is what I base my estimate on. Also how many men would comprise a reserve brigade also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that's -- by the book, that's the number of men who should be in a brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Approximately that number of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware that some units in the JNA had desertion rates of as high as 90 per cent? That kind of attrition? Did you know that was going on?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that now?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I know it because you've just told me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I was go about to get to my feet and object to the form of that question. There is no evidence at all before this Court at this time that that's what the rate --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There certainly is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is something that was mentioned about a month ago by one of the witnesses, and I think there was a document which specified that there was heavy -- quite a considerable desertion -- not 90 per cent, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't recall any evidence that there was 90 per cent desertion in July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 90 per cent is being suggested by Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we did see a document in which it was alleged that desertion --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Was rampant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I took the witness through the document myself but I don't recall any recollection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 90 per cent, no, 90 per cent is Mr. Ackerman's assessment. He comes from Texas, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My recollection is this. The strength of the unit this person commanded -- I think it was supposed to be 1500 and I think there were 78 people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... To the bare essentials. I mean, I think he's answered you in a way which should be enough for you to proceed to the next question because more or less you know what value you would give to his assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A bit further down in the same paragraph, sir, you say there were two tanks on Redak hill, isn't it the case that you later said, well, there was really only one tank on Redak hill?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I think to this very day that there were two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever tell anybody that you were mistaken about that and that you really only knew of one tank there?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I don't remember. Perhaps I said that one tank could be clearly seen, that it could be clearly seen, but judging by the detonations and the firing, I think that it was clear that there were two tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On page 10 of the English version of the statement, it begins -- there is a paragraph that begins with, "Regarding interethnic relations of Croats and Serbs." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. I know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you say in there that it was only in 1991, two years before you gave this statement, that Serbs started calling themselves Serbs, that before that, they had called themselves Vlasi or Orthodox. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That was the usual thing. We called ourselves Sokci and when they came to our villages, they would say that they were going to the Sokcis' and we would say that we were going to the Vlasi but this was not taken in any derogatory way and it wasn't taken in a bad way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So, what you're saying is it's true that Serbs didn't call themselves Serbs until 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The majority of those that I know, whom I socialised with and worked with, became, let me put it that way, hard-core -- they became only Serbs and nothing else during those years. Before it wasn't so important. Most frequently we would call ourselves Vlasi, Sokci, Muslims. Only later did this polarisation come about that they called themselves only Serbs and nothing else, and then on our Croatian, the Sokac side, we became only Croats and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that during that period of 1992, that you did not, yourself, personally, witness the commission of any crime?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can we make it clear what period of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The spring of 1992, when you're talking about the attack on Brisevo, the events that you've been -- you have spoken about in your direct testimony. Isn't it true that during that period you were not an eyewitness to any crime?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It's true that I was the eyewitness to the killing of a person called Pero Dimac. I saw the killing and torture of that person myself, from a distance of 15 to 20 metres at the most. The other actual killings, I did not see. And this is clearly stated somewhere in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, again, I find myself confused and I'm going to ask you to help me. There is a statement, and I don't know quite how to identify it, it's got an ERN number of 03042383 in the English version. It's a statement that involves questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Incidentally, I didn't know whether anyone was going to refer to this statement. But I had in mind to draw the attention of you, Ms. Korner, in particular, that I have -- before I allow any questions on this statement, I need a clarification. It seems that this statement is made by Ivo Simo Atlija, born on the 3rd of March, 1929. If that is the case, it's certainly not the witness that we have, because the witness was born on the 19th of May of 1963.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the best thing is if the witness -- if Your Honour can perhaps -- or I can, can be asked if he knows who Ivo Simo Atlija, born on the 3rd of March, 1929, was -- is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also I wouldn't like to mention the residence, the address, but perhaps if the document is shown to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think perhaps he can help -- I didn't see --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if it is not this witness who made this statement, I have no interest in asking questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman I was waiting for someone to refer to this statement because until that happened, I was not considering it as being tendered in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think one of the difficulties is when the searches are does you quite often get somebody with the same first and second name. I hadn't picked up that clearly this hadn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know of anyone Ivanka Atlija. Do you know of anyone by the name of Ivanka Atlija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the witness can tell us who this man is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know both the mentioned persons, Mr. Ivo, the son of Simo, Atlija is my cousin. He's an elderly man. You said that you don't need the address but I could tell you the address. And the woman that you mentioned, Ivanka Atlija, I know her. I am Ivo Atlija, the son of Ilija, that's how you can tell us apart and he's the son of Simo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do we need this document, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ackerman, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The document I suppose should be removed from Your Honour's packets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You don't have to worry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to now go to some of your testimony in the Stakic case, sir. And I'm now going to refer to page, for the record, 5557 of your testimony. You talk there about seeing the events and the fighting at Hambarine and being able to observe that, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there was shooting coming from both sides there, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Correct. There was shooting from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you told the Court in Stakic was that when the shots would come from Hambarine the Serb soldiers moving forward would lie down?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. I said that. And I said that that I didn't know whether that was because they were hit and wounded or whether they were just seeking shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We are now going to speak about the Brisevo situation. You spoke about 24th of June, 1992, when some arrests were made in Brisevo. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And these arrests were actually made by police officers, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's right. They were wearing blue police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you told the Court in Stakic that one of those police officers involved in those arrests was a Croat by the name of Bjekic or that you at least thought he was a Croat. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. That's true. I think he's a Croat by ethnicity and I think that his number -- his name is not Jekic but Bjekic. There is a "B" at the beginning of his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I said Bjekic. At least I'm looking at the word Bjekic. I hope I said that. But in any event your answer is correct. I want you to see P1523. That's this map again. Do you still have it? Do you still have it over there?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your testimony, you talked about a day when you went from Brisevo to go swimming. Can you show us on the map where you went to go swimming?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I can show it to you even though that little lake is not marked here. It's somewhere here. It belongs to the village of Stara Rijeka and they are actually -- the lake is something that was created after the ore was dug so it's a hole from where ore was extracted and then later, a lake is formed in that hole.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you had talked earlier in your testimony about how your village was completely blockaded, that you almost felt like you were under siege in your village, and how the only food you could get was what was available in the village and that you could get out of gardens and things of that nature. I'm wondering how it is that you could leave your village and go off swimming at Stara Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We could go because this pool was closer to Brisevo, and it was further away from the road from Stara Rijeka to Ljubija, and that was the road that was under the control of Serb soldiers. We were able to get to the road, the pool was before you got to the road. So we could go to the pool and swim and do other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you just showed us on the map, unless you were wrong, to go from Brisevo to where you said the pool was, you have to cross at least one road. Am I wrong about that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No, you're not wrong. You could go and -- down one road. There are also roads here that are not marked on the map at all. They are local roads, and I mentioned in the statement that the map is not very precise because it was drawn by hand. This is not a topographical map where I could locate down to one metre where something was, where the road was, where the pool was, where the river was, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, just seems to me if you could leave the village to go off swimming you could also leave the village to go off and get food, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That is only something that you think. Somebody tried to go to Gornja Ravska village and he was beaten up and returned. They also waited for him on the road that leads from Ljubija to Stara Rijeka and where the road to Gornja Ravska branches off.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you went to Stara Rijeka to go swimming, I assume you came back home and in that trip, were you ever beaten up?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I did not encounter anybody on that road who would beat me up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There came a time when the Serbs were demanding that your village, Brisevo, surrender a weapon called a Bofors, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's right. First we were shelled for one day, and then they set terms that we should surrender all our weapons, including the Bofors gun which was something that we never even had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And your understanding of that weapon, I think is that it's a three-barrel anti-aircraft weapon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And isn't it the case that the Serbs believed that you had that gun because a Croat by the name of Nikola Juric told them that you did?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I also heard that information later. Nikola Juric from Gornja Ravska, if that's the person you're thinking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the person I'm thinking of. Do you know -- did he just make that story up or had there once been such a gun in Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: In all of my 30 years of life at Brisevo, I never saw such a gun, not even when military exercises were being conducted, and there were such exercises sometimes at Brisevo so there was never any gun like that used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to now talk about the two meetings that you had with Vojo Kupresanin. There was one around the middle of August and at the time you had that meeting, you knew I take it that Vojo Kupresanin was president of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said in your testimony in Stakic that he said that he was the President of the Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina. You know that there was no entity called the Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina, don't you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: At that time, names were changed overnight. There was the Serb Autonomous Region, Krajina, Autonomous Region Krajina, Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and eventually Republika Srpska. Whether at that time it was the official name Autonomous Region of Krajina or the Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina I really wouldn't be able to tell you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know there was never an entity called the Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that it never existed. I even think that such an official name was mentioned somewhere, whether you can find it in some document, on a piece of paper, I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The answer is you don't know but you think you heard that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your meetings with Kupresanin, you begged him to help you leave Brisevo and cross the Croatian border, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you said to him, in your testimony you said, "We asked to be -- to let us leave from there, that the killings should stop, that they wanted that territory, then they should keep it." Right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Right. I said if they wanted that territory so let them have it but just let those much beleaguered people leave that area and stop the killing because it couldn't end up in anything good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony at page 5643, you said, "We asked to be -- to let us leave from there." When you say, "We asked," did you ask? Or did somebody else ask on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I talked with Mr. Kupresanin personally, and I was speaking in my own name and the name of the survivors of Brisevo, that is why I said, "We want to leave," not only myself but all those who had survived in Brisevo wanted to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Kupresanin was apparently unable to help you in that regard, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin promised to help us as best as he could, that he would first intercede with General Talic because individuals, a group of soldiers, continued to come and persecute us and loot us, even after those killings, he said that he would intercede with General Talic, that it would end, that he would do whatever he could do but that he would help us to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, in fact what he told you was that he couldn't help you leave the area, that you should go see Milomir Stakic about that, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: He said that for assistance, that we could ask for assistance from Mr. Stakic, and if nothing came out of that, and if we couldn't leave then, then he gave us his telephone number and promised that we'd be ail to make a phone call from the headquarters -- from the Serb headquarters in Ljubija, that is what he promised. We could go to Ljubija, back and forth, two or three of us, we could make our phone calls from Mr. Kupresanin or from Bishop Komarica's office or from Caritas's office. Nobody stopped us from doing that but unfortunately at that time we still were not able to leave that area, unfortunately at that time we could not do that yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's the case, isn't it, that Bishop Komarica, who was also there, opposed you in your efforts to leave the area, didn't he? He didn't want you to leave?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: He thought that we should stay at all cost in the area because the Croats had lived there for more than 700 years, that our homesteads were there, the graves of our forefathers were, that it was our turf, which in a way is all true, but we thought we believed that if it was better to leave and survive rather than stay and get killed on our turf.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But the other thing that you talked to Mr. Kupresanin about was the violence going on on that territory and how the killing needed to be stopped and what he told you was that he would talk with General Talic and try to intercede and to get the situation under control, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know if he ever talked to General Talic?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No. I don't. I don't know if he talked with General Talic personally but when he came to Ljubija the next time, he bid me to come aside and asked me what the situation was, has anything been done to improve the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: And I told him that nothing had changed except that Juro Dimac and Zdenka Lovric and I could freely go to Ljubija to make phone calls.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So he -- can we conclude that one of two things happened? He either did not take it up with General Talic or General Talic was unable to effect any kind of a change?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, I could agree with you that it was -- yes, that one of those two possibilities is what probably happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was a second occasion, then, that you saw Kupresanin at the Ljubija church, right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Right. In front of the church, not inside the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And again you asked him to help you move out of there and that you were willing to go just about anywhere? Correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Correct. And Kupresanin told us again that he'd help us in so far as he could do that. He even offered that two or three of us could go to Banja Luka that he would put us into a hotel and from there it would be easier for us to establish contact with the UNPROFOR or whatever other organisation, whatever they were called, through which we could perhaps leave, that is move out of that territory. However, we never went to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether he helped any other people that way or not, by taking them to Banja Luka and then getting them help to leave from there? Do you know about anybody else that was helped by Mr. Kupresanin in that way?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No, I don't, because with other -- what shall I call them, refugees, victims of those war, we had no contact. We were not in touch with them. We could go make phone calls to Dr. Stakic, no, sorry, we could make phone calls from Mr. Kupresanin's office or from Bishop Komarica's office but we had nobody else in Banja Luka to get in touch with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were actually finally able to leave, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. Eventually, at long last, after a lot of red tape, payments and negotiations, persuasions, yes, thank God, we managed to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 5655 of your testimony in Stakic, you were asked this question: "Did you have to sign any documents before you left?" And the answer you gave, and I'm quoting, sir, "We were supposed to sign that we were leaving of our own free will and then also sign a certificate leaving our property at the disposal of I can't remember whether it was called Republika Srpska or the Autonomous Region of Serbian Krajina at that point. I can't say with certainty now." Did you actually then didn't wind up signing a document? You were supposed to but you didn't? Is that -- am I -- am I interpreting that answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No. I don't think you are. We had to sign these documents, all these documents that we had paid our electricity, water and whatever other bills. We had to hand them over at the secretariat of the interior in Prijedor and in exchange we received from them a paper which was the authorisation to move out and even that paper was seized from us as we mounted the buses when the convoy was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you actually signed a piece of paper leaving your property at the disposal of some government?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And let me ask you this: In terms of preservation, do you think it would be better to just abandon your property and leave it totally unattended or to leave it at the disposal of and in the custody of a government agency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the president, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want to hear what I think about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour, I do. He was asked and he should be allowed to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now that the question has been put and allowed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Okay. I personally think that only I and my lawyer, my solicitors or somebody else I authorise may dispose of my property and nobody else. But since at that time the lives of 300 or more people were in question, they were worth more than all the property there. I mean, I think that these people are worth more than all the property in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I mean any material value, I do not think that there is any material value that can be compared in terms of its worth with the human life. That is what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that by the Dayton Accords that you could go back there today and request your property back and it would have to be given to you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of so-called certificates about surrendering property have been proclaimed invalid and vacated. I am aware that I could get my property back, and some of these things are also in the hands of lawyers in Prijedor. But I think that nothing will come out of this return.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were asked a question by Ms. Korner at the end of your testimony about whether you even wanted to return or not. I want to know if you know that according to the authorities, I think it's SFOR or maybe Mr. Ashdown's office, I'm not sure, but according to one of those authorities, one of the easiest and safest places to return to is the Prijedor municipality. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a reference to that reference? Which report you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the report you attached to the witness protection motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I have an actual quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't have the exact quote. I don't have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I may have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have it available, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, but Ms. Gustin is having a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know I don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour, I won't pursue this. The question has been asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go. Perhaps I could ask the witness whether he feels he will agree with that assessment irrespective of where it's coming from. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the question is asked. I think the witness is ready to answer if we just let him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The question, sir, was this: You were asked a question by Ms. Korner at the end of your testimony about whether you even wanted to return or not. I want to know if you know that according to authorities, I think it's SFOR, that's, you know what SFOR is or maybe Mr. -- Lord Ashdown's office, I'm not sure, but according to one of those authorities, one of the easiest and safest places to return to is the Prijedor municipality. Are you aware of that? Lord Ashdown had nothing to do with that assessment and neither did SFOR by the way, Mr. Ackerman. That was the office that the Tribunal has which monitors situations from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was, Your Honour, it was one of the UN organisations, nothing to do with your office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you found it, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to be precise so if you could let me look at it, the precise language so the record is clear as to what the precise language actually is because I'm working from memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think you ought to put the precise language.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would love to. I'm very anxious to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir, what I'm looking at is a document called a security assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was filed confidentially and we are in open session. Could we just not refer to where it emanates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner is right or we go to private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go to private session for a moment because I think it might be important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to private session. Private session, Ms. Chuqing, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, with regard to Prijedor, the report says this: "Prijedor has been open to returns since 1998 and remains one of the best return sites in the RS. Returns are estimated at over 8.000 for the entire municipality, with returnees continuing to come back every day. The current mayor is moderate and has been very cooperative with the international community. The security situation for returnees is generally good, although there have been mostly minor incidents until now. Recent return-related incidents involve explosions near the homes of returnees and the Imam in town. The explosions are not limited to returnee sites, though, as the majority of the incidents are more likely related to local organised crime. The Bosniak community here is now strong enough to enable Bosniaks to testify with more confidence although the risk for a Bosniak or Croat testifying against a Serb is still considerable. The Serb community continues to harbour hard-line elements. The risk for a Serb from Prijedor testifying against a Bosniak or Croat is minimal." Now that's the report and the question I really asked you was were you aware that it was one of the best return sites for people wanting to return? And I take it you were not aware until I read that to you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I was not aware of this perception of the situation but let me tell you why I do not want, and I think cannot go back there. At the time of exhumation of people killed in Brisevo and the funeral, one of the policemen who allegedly was there to look after our security, the policeman of the Republika Srpska, he was one of the policemen who participated in the attack on Brisevo. I recognised him. Secondly, during the exhumation, during the exhumation itself, when one body was taken out of the ground and it was in a pretty good condition, not decomposed that is, and one of the Serb policemen said, "Fuck his Ustasha mother, he's still bleeding after ten years." Such men cannot guarantee my security. I want to protect myself from them and also to protect them against themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know, don't you, that there were horrible things that happened in that area in World War II? Massacres of immense proportion, you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Relevance, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, relevance, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It has to do with the answer he just gave, Your Honour, and I think the next question will make it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear the next question too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said that before the war, interethnic relations amongst different groups was extremely good. My question is: How did it happen that after those horrible events of World War II, that interethnic relations became good in view of what you just told us about your concern that they will never become good after what happened in 1992? What was different?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The difference, I wouldn't be able to tell you about the difference because I was born some 20 years after World War II. I do not know what was the set of -- what was the state of mind and what kind of political tensions or differences existed amongst different groups following World War II. I am aware that many, many crimes were committed against the Serb population during World War II but I was born 20 years later. Most of those people who attacked Brisevo were also born 20, 30 or even more years after World War II. I have nothing to do with that and I therefore cannot -- I cannot really comment on something like that. I cannot make any appraisals of the situation or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the Stakic trial, Judge Vassylenko asked you to name persons involved in propaganda activities in the region, and your answer to Judge Vassylenko was that there was a journalist from Radio Prijedor and Kozarski Vjesnik by the name of Milan Mutic. I believe that's the person you named being involved in the propaganda activities. Am I right about that? Did I read that properly because it was a bit confusing?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. You did, but it's not the same Milan Mutic whom I mentioned in a part of my statement that he had misappropriated my flat. They are two different persons called the same, though. There were more of them. But I know the name of Milan Mutic because that is a person whom I personally -- whom I know personally, unfortunately he wasn't the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But that was the answer you gave Judge Vassylenko regarding who was involved and responsible for the propaganda, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all I have, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I suppose there is a re-examination, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, there is, Your Honour. Mr. Trbojevic is on his feet for some reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I see. I recognise Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, part of a witness's answer is not in the transcript and the video was on and so Mr. Ackerman did not see. On page 58, line 21, with reference to the existence or non-existence of an anti-aircraft gun, the witness said that unfortunately they did not have it. And that is not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "Unfortunately, we did not have it?" Is this what you mean, that he said, used the term, the word "unfortunately" and this does not show in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You've heard what Mr. Trbojevic has just stated. When you were being asked a question about the Bofors gun, did you actually state, "Unfortunately we did not have it"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer was, "We did not have such a gun, now I think unfortunately we did not have it, because had we had it, we then would have been in a position to return it. We cannot return something that we do not have."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Trbojevic. What I suggest is we give the technicians four minutes to change the tape because it should be coming up any time now. We have been sitting for almost an hour and a half, and we remain here and you proceed with your re-examination. Is that all right with the interpreters? Okay? All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't got that much in re-examination but there is there any point in trying to start Ms. Sutherland's witness since 6.00? He's been in the room since 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know how long Ms. Sutherland anticipates this witness to last. How much time she needs. Because.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We still have 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland won't finish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't expect her to finish the witness today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: She can certainly start him. I've got about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed with your re-examination then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, it was put to you or you were asked about your evidence respect of the surrender of this so-called Bofors gun. Were you asked to surrender that gun before or after the village was initially shelled on the 27th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he already gave the answer that it was after the village had been shelled. I don't think it needs to be repeated. When I asked him the question he said it was after the village had first been shelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I want to make -- I want to counter a point which I think is going to be made that the attack on Brisevo was connected with this gun so I want to just deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Proceed, Ms. Korner. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, the attack, the shelling of Brisevo, on the 27th of May, had there been any request for the surrender of a Bofors gun or other weapons before that initial shelling?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Before the shelling, there was no demand to hand over the Bofors. Only when our delegation went to Rasavci to see why they were firing at us, then they said what they were looking for. They presented it as an example of what would happen to us if we do not surrender weapons, including that infamous Bofors.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've told us over and over again you didn't have such a weapon. Did you hand over to them such hunting rifles and pistols as you had?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The weapons that we did have were loaded on to a small tractor. There wasn't more than ten of such weapons. I don't know the exact number. And this was given to the soldiers at the checkpoint at Donja Ravska. We even received some kind of certificate, receipt, but I don't know who has this receipt, whether it was thrown away or destroyed. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, between the 27th of May, or thereabouts, and the all-out attack on the 24th of July, were there any other requests or demands for the handing over of the Bofors gun?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: When these weapons that we had were taken away and handed over, the Serb soldiers or the Serb authorities, whoever there was responsible for that, said that their delegation would come to run a house-by-house search in the village, that some of the villagers had to be present and that a house where weapons were found would be burned. The owner would be killed. And if they don't find any weapons at Brisevo, any weapons or the Bofors, then that nothing would happen to us. But they kept talking about this Bofors, Bofors.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were any house-to-house searches carried out by members of the Serb police or military or the authorities generally?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No, no one ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've told us how -- or you told the Court in Stakic how you were awoken at 3.00 a.m. on the 24th of July by the sound of shelling. Before that, either immediately or in the week before that, had there been any demand made to surrender weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had there been any announcements made over radio or megaphone that the Serbs were -- had reason to believe that you were in possession of arms and that unless you surrendered them, your village would be shelled?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you given any kind of warning that the shelling was to take place?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No. We were never given any warning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Any opportunity to take, at least send from the village, the women, the children, the old, the elderly, the infirm?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We didn't have any means to do it. We didn't know where to go, how to go. Allow me to explain. There was no petrol and the few cars or tractors and other transport means that we had, for example, we were not in a position to be able to buy gas or oil so even if we were -- if it was possible for us to go, we could only go on foot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had you -- had anybody in your village attempted any kind of attack or resistance to what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just -- I object to this. I just can't imagine how this was raised by anything I asked on cross-examination. It's brand new direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, with respect, he's not. Unless -- what I'm dealing with is, I anticipate, a suggestion being made that this village was shelled on the 24th of July because in some ways this was connected with the Bofors gun. Otherwise, what was the purpose of Mr. Ackerman's cross-examination on the Bofors gun?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That point you have made. Now you have -- you are proceeding further. You're suggesting that a further point in your argument, a further step, which I don't think is fair because he never suggested that the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Fine, if Your Honour there is not going to be any suggestion at any stage in this case that the attack on Brisevo on the 24th of July was anything other than an unprovoked attack then I'm content and I won't take this further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's a completely different matter, Your Honour. And if she wanted to make sure that there wasn't going to be any such thing she should have done that in direct. She had her direct examination. She finished with it. What she's doing now is not raised by my cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your objection is sustained. Let's move to the next question. Forget about whether there was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I just want to make absolutely clear and we are back to the good old Rule 90(H). If there is going to be evidence called or in any stage going to be suggested that this attack resulted from something that was done by them, then that should have been put to this witness and it hasn't so I will leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was no suggestion forthcoming from Mr. -- At least during his cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm content with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Neither does it appear from the documents that I have read that any such thing sort of happened in the case of his village or town or whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, I just want to deal then, please, with one other matter and that's the question of your property. You lived in Prijedor before the takeover on the 30th of April. What happened to your property?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: As I said, several times before, Milan Mutic moved into my apartment, who lived in Donja Ljubija. Before that, it wasn't possible for me to move around, normally, I wasn't able to return to Prijedor because -- because -- without the permission of the authorities in Ljubija, it was not possible to travel. The house in Brisevo was burned to the ground. And all of the things of value that we had in the house were -- and also, the immovable property around the house, so all of the property owned not only by myself but my whole family and my mother and my father, all of that was destroyed, all of the property that I managed to bring out of Brisevo, or Prijedor, amounts to one pair of shoes, one pair of trousers, one T-shirt, and one jeans jacket. That was the entire property that I took with me when I left that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The suggestion was made to you that wasn't it preferable to sign over all your property to the custody of the -- in inverted commas -- government. In normal circumstances, would you have been prepared to hand over your property to the state?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No, not to any state. I own my property and not the state.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Your Honour, that's all I ask in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What's wrong, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Nothing wrong, Your Honour I just have an additional question based on the re-examination by Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Korner asked him if they had been warned in any way that Brisevo was going to be attacked and he said no. And in fact, on the day that he went swimming, a Serb came there and told them that the next day, their village was going to be attacked and warned him that that was going to happen. And it's in the Stakic transcript. Your Honours will find it there. I don't necessarily need to ask him the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, but what I was asking about was not some Serb neighbour kindly warning them, "you're about to be attacked," but any official warnings from any kind of governmental thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you need to answer it because we already had the answer. So let's conclude with this witness. Mr. Atlija, I thank you on behalf of this Tribunal for having accepted to come over a second time to give evidence at this time in this trial, previously in the Stakic trial. You will be attended to by the staff of this Tribunal to help you return to your place of residence. And now you will be escorted by the usher. Thank you. Now, Ms. Korner and Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to stop in any case to enable the technicians to change the tape. I promised everyone to finish in time to -- as requested. Ms. Sutherland, do you prefer to start today or what do you -- what is your preference? How long -- do you think tomorrow's sitting will be enough for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think I estimated last night possibly three-quarters of an hour. I think I may be an hour and a half. I want to show a couple of videotapes to the witness and what I wanted to possibly even try and do either this evening or tomorrow was admit the photographs and maps from the prior witness so we can do that first thing in the morning, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the afternoon, yeah. And Mr. Ackerman, do you plan to have a lengthy cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Depending on how the witness answers questions, it should be about the same as today. Length wise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Pretty close to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't, in any event, got another witness because the witness who starts on Monday is a lengthy witness and he's got to listen to days and days of tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I think we can stop now, all right? Would someone please explain to the witness, if he's been here waiting, that this is not due to any disregard to his -- who is going to take care of that? You will take care of that? Okay. Thank you. So I thank everyone. This is the end of today's sitting. We adjourn until tomorrow in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 5.42 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 22nd day of November, 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
